case_name: Pohalya Motya Valvi v State of Maharashtra

State of Maharashtra

facts: The appeal arises from a judgment rendered by the High Court of Bombay in Criminal Appeal No. 1329 of 1971 filed by the State of Maharashtra against the judgment of the Sessions Judge, Dhulia, setting aside his acquittal and convicting the appellant for having committed an offence under Section 302, Indian Penal Code, 1860 and sentencing him to suffer imprisonment for life.

The case depends on circumstantial evidence. As the case depends on circumstantial evidence, at the outset the well established principles governing the appreciation of evidence in a case dependent upon circumstantial evidence may be borne in mind.
The first and the second circumstances relied upon by the High Court can be examined together.
Undoubtedly thereafter deceased was not seen alive by anyone but two persons were in company of the deceased, viz., appellant and Bhamta when they left the house of Bhikjya.

It is alleged that the appellant did not return home till the next morning and when he returned to the house in the early hours of the morning he was alone and when questioned by Motibai, PW 4, the widow of the deceased, he offered a false explanation.

Evidence of PSI, D. K. Patil, the investigating officer is that he arrested the appellant who was already in custody of the police Patil on October 3, 1970 and attached arts. 8 to 11 from the person of the appellant being the clothes of the appellant which appeared to be stained with blood.
issues: What are the principles governing the appreciation of evidence in a case dependent upon circumstantial evidence?

Is the fact that the accused and the deceased were last seen alive in company of each other and the failure of the accused to satisfactorily account for the disappearance of the deceased considered a circumstance of an incriminating character?
What is the evidentiary value of the circumstances Nos. 3 and 4?
Is the information given by the appellant after his arrest leading to the discovery of the spear which was found to be stained with human blood, a circumstance of clinching character?
petitioner_arguments: The prosecution case rests on circumstantial evidence.

Each circumstance relied upon by the prosecution must be established by cogent, succinct and reliable evidence; that the circumstance relied upon must be such as cannot be explained on any hypothesis except the guilt of the accused.
court_reasoning: The High Court was of the opinion that no other view is possible except that the appellant was responsible for the murder of the deceased.
It is better to reproduce them so that the examination becomes pertinent, pin-pointed and confined within narrow limits.
Accordingly, circumstances Nos. 3 and 4 have no evidentiary value.
holding: The High Court convicted the appellant for having committed an offence under Section 302, Indian Penal Code, 1860 and sentenced him to suffer imprisonment for life.
